summary: Extends the Network Services Monitoring MIB so mail transfer agents can be monitored, and can also be used for monitoring MTA components inside gateways. It was replaced by RFC 2249, RFC 2789.

eli5.summary: This lists gauges on a mail delivery program, so a manager can see how many messages it is handling.

questions: monitor mail transfer agents with snmp
how many messages in a mail queue
subtitle: Monitoring message delivery systems with SNMP gauges and counters

tldr.problem: Network administrators need to monitor mail transfer agents to see how many messages they are processing, how much data they are handling, and whether there are problems with message delivery.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1566 defines a set of management objects using SNMP that track messages received, stored, and transmitted, as well as volumes and recipient counts at both the overall MTA level and per group level.
tldr.outcome: Administrators can query live statistics from their mail servers using standard SNMP tools. The MIB was later refined by RFC 2249 and RFC 2789.

today: RFC 1566 is a Proposed Standard. It was obsoleted by RFC 2249 and RFC 2789, which refined the mail monitoring approach.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 1566 extends the Network Services Monitoring MIB to add monitoring capabilities for Message Transfer Agents (MTAs). An MTA is a mail server that receives messages from users and other MTAs, decides where each message should go next, and delivers it onward.

The MIB provides a standardized way to ask a mail server questions about its operation using SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol). Administrators can find out how many messages the MTA has received since startup, how many are currently waiting to be sent, and how much data has been moved through the system.
sections.eli5: An MTA is the post office that handles your email. This MIB is the form you fill out to ask the post office how many letters came in today, how many are waiting to go out, and how much work it is doing.

sections.title: Message Flow and MTA Structure
sections.content:
Messages flow through an MTA in four steps: they are received from users or other MTAs, the next hop is determined (where the message goes next), the message is converted to the right format for that destination, and it is transmitted onward. Messages may be stored at different points in this process depending on how the MTA is designed.

The MIB divides monitoring into two levels. The MTA table tracks totals across the entire server: messages received, stored, and transmitted; the total volume in kilo-octets; and the count of recipients. The MTA group table breaks these down by functional group, allowing admins to see which parts of the system (for example, inbound mail or outbound mail to a particular domain) are handling the most traffic.
sections.eli5: Email comes in, gets sorted, might wait in a holding area, and then goes out. The monitoring system counts all of this at two levels: the whole post office, and each station inside it.

sections.title: Overall MTA Counters
sections.content:
The MTA table provides nine objects. mtaReceivedMessages counts all messages that have arrived since the MTA started. mtaStoredMessages is a snapshot of how many are sitting in the queue right now. mtaTransmittedMessages counts all messages sent out since startup.

The RFC also tracks volume: mtaReceivedVolume, mtaStoredVolume, and mtaTransmittedVolume measure the total size of message data in kilo-octets at each stage. Finally, mtaReceivedRecipients, mtaStoredRecipients, and mtaTransmittedRecipients count the total number of addresses (recipients) involved in all messages at each stage. These counts may not always line up perfectly because messages may be duplicated or expanded as they move through the system.
sections.eli5: The server counts three kinds of things: how many complete messages, how big they are in total, and how many addresses they are going to. It counts each of these as messages arrive, wait, and leave.

sections.title: Group-Level Monitoring
sections.content:
The MTA group table tracks the same kinds of counters as the overall table but divided by functional group. MTAs often organize their work into groups for inbound handling, queue storage, and outbound delivery to different destinations. Each group can optionally report rejected messages, the age of the oldest message in its queue, the number of active and accumulated associations (connections) to and from other systems, and reasons for recent failures.

For example, if an MTA has groups for SMTP-based delivery and X.400-based delivery, the group table lets an admin monitor each separately. The mtaGroupName field identifies which remote MTA or domain the group connects to. The group table also reports mtaGroupMailProtocol, which identifies whether the group uses SMTP, X.400, or another protocol.
sections.eli5: If the post office has different stations for different types of mail (like local delivery, national delivery, and international), each station has its own set of counters so you can see how busy each one is.

sections.title: Associations and Failures
sections.content:
At the group level, the MIB tracks associations—active connections to other MTAs or clients. mtaGroupInboundAssociations is the current count of clients or MTAs sending mail to this group. mtaGroupOutboundAssociations is the current count of connections the group is using to deliver mail elsewhere. Cumulative counters track total associations since the MTA started.

When things go wrong, the MIB reports mtaGroupRejectedInboundAssociations and mtaGroupFailedOutboundAssociations**, and stores the reason for the last failure in text fields. The mtaGroupScheduledRetry field tells you when the MTA will next try to reach a failed destination. This information helps admins diagnose delivery problems.
sections.eli5: The server counts how many phone lines (connections) are open right now, and how many have failed. When a connection fails, it writes down why, so you know what went wrong.
